subject: 99656E1B1D7344D8930ACA530FDE210B
introduction: The guide returns again and again to one principle: religion must agree with science and reason, and a belief that cannot bear their examination is superstition. A hundred of its quotations are read here with a hundred from elsewhere. Many say the same in older words: Paul’s ‘prove all things’, the Bereans who searched the scriptures daily, the Qur’an’s refusal of conjecture and of what the fathers followed, Aquinas on grace perfecting nature, Browne’s two books, Locke’s last judge, Milton’s open contest between truth and falsehood. Others stand on the far side of the question. Tertullian asks what Athens has to do with Jerusalem; Paul warns against philosophy and against science falsely so called; Kant makes room for belief by limiting knowledge; Hume and Spinoza press reason further into scripture than most believers would follow; Whitman, Keats and Wordsworth fear what analysis does to wonder. Where the guide turns to material progress without spiritual progress, Thoreau, Mill, Arnold and Eisenhower speak beside it. The contrasts are there so that the principle can be tested, which is what it asks for.
questions: The guide calls a religion that contradicts science superstition. How would you tell a belief that contradicts reason from one that reason has not yet reached?
Joshua's sun and the psalm's unmoving world were once read as astronomy. What do Origen, Paul and the Qur'an's distinction between clear and allegorical verses suggest about reading such passages?
Tertullian and Paul warn against philosophy, and Aquinas and Browne welcome it. What was each afraid of, and what was each hoping for?
Bacon says the understanding is no dry light. What habits would keep either a scientist or a believer honest about what they would prefer to be true?
The guide says science cannot by itself create fellowship or cure the body politic. Which of the outside voices on machinery and progress do you find most persuasive, and why?
Whitman leaves the lecture room to look at the stars in silence. What does the image of two wings ask of a person who is drawn more to one kind of knowing than the other?

outside.why: Aquinas states the agreement from the side of theology: grace does not destroy nature but perfects it, so natural reason should minister to faith.
Tertullian asks what Athens has to do with Jerusalem, or the Academy with the Church. What did he fear from joining the two, and what is lost by keeping them apart?
Paul's rule for his churches is short: prove all things, and hold fast that which is good.
The Buddha tells the Kalamas not to go by reports, legends, traditions or scripture, nor even by logical conjecture and inference.
Browne collects his divinity from two books, the written one of God and that of his servant Nature, which lies open to the eyes of all.
Tennyson asks for both together: let knowledge grow from more to more, but more of reverence dwell in us.
John's Gospel makes truth itself the liberator: ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.
Peter asks believers to be ready always to give an answer to anyone who asks a reason of the hope that is in them.
In the book of Joshua the sun stands still and the moon stays at a man's word. Is such a passage teaching astronomy, and who decides how it is to be read?
Whitman grows tired and sick among the astronomer's proofs and figures, and goes out to look up in silence at the stars. Is that a quarrel with science, or with one way of teaching it?
Jesus charges his critics with laying aside the commandment of God in order to hold the tradition of men.
Pascal holds that the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know. Must everything a person rightly believes be something they can comprehend?
The first commandment as Jesus gives it asks for love of God with all the heart, all the soul and all the mind.
The Bereans are called more noble because they searched the scriptures daily to see whether the things they heard were so.
Paul warns the Colossians against being spoiled through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men. Is the warning against thinking, or against one kind of thinking?
Aristotle opens with the same conviction: all men by nature desire to know, as the delight we take in our senses shows.
Proverbs calls it the glory of God to conceal a thing, and the honour of kings to search out a matter.
An early verse of the Qur'an describes God as the one who teaches man that which he knew not.
Locke puts the principle in a single sentence: reason must be our last judge and guide in every thing.
Kant said he had to abolish knowledge in order to make room for belief. Does faith need a region that reason cannot enter, or one that it can?
Bacon observed that a little philosophy inclines man's mind to atheism, while depth in philosophy brings it round again.
Paul warns Timothy against oppositions of science falsely so called. Who is to judge when a science is false: its own methods, or the faith it troubles?
The psalm makes inquiry a pleasure of the devout: the works of the Lord are great, sought out of all who delight in them.
Isaiah hears the invitation from God's own side: come now, and let us reason together.
Paul calls the Athenians too superstitious and then begins from their own altar to the unknown God. Is superstition better met by rejection, or by finding what it was reaching for?
The Qur'an forbids following that of which one has no knowledge, and says the hearing, the sight and the heart will each be asked.
The Qur'an says that most people follow nothing but conjecture, and that conjecture cannot take the place of truth.
Proverbs distinguishes the simple, who believe every word, from the prudent, who look well to their going.
Hume would accept testimony to a miracle only if its falsehood would be more miraculous than the fact. Is that the test the guide asks religion to pass, or a stricter one?
Milton trusts an open contest: let truth and falsehood grapple, for who ever knew truth put to the worse in a free encounter?
Bacon says that human knowledge and human power meet in one. If science is to be a handmaid, whom does that power serve, and who decides?
Proverbs sees one wisdom at work in both: by wisdom the Lord founded the earth, and by his knowledge the depths are broken up.
The book of Daniel counts knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom as gifts of God to four young men.
Paul names a sound mind, together with power and love, as what God has given in place of the spirit of fear.
Emerson's sentence states the mirror in a line: every natural fact is a symbol of some spiritual fact.
Xenophanes remarked that oxen, horses and lions, if they had hands and could paint, would give the gods bodies like their own.
Newton writes that we have no idea of the substance of God, and know him only by his most wise and excellent contrivances of things.
The Qur'an reports the reply 'we follow that wherein we found our fathers' and asks: even though their fathers were unintelligent and unguided?
Descartes resolved never to accept anything for true which he did not clearly know to be such. Could any religion, or any science, live by that rule alone?
Wordsworth thinks one impulse from a vernal wood may teach more of moral evil and of good than all the sages can. What does that kind of knowing owe to reason?
Hosea's charge against his own people is that they are destroyed for lack of knowledge.
The proverb says flatly that for the soul to be without knowledge is not good.
The Qur'an calls the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of night and day, tokens for men of understanding.
The Qur'an promises portents on the horizons and within themselves, until it is manifest to them that it is the truth.
Tennyson finds more faith in honest doubt than in half the creeds. Is a religion that has passed through doubt the same religion afterwards?
John's letter tells believers not to believe every spirit, but to try the spirits whether they are of God.
Hamlet reasons that he that made us did not give us capability and godlike reason to fust in us unused.
Paul says God has made foolish the wisdom of this world, which by wisdom knew not God. How does that sit with a religion that is asked to satisfy reason?
Paul calls the offering of oneself to God, holy and acceptable, a reasonable service.
The psalm uses the same image of the word: its entrance gives light, and it gives understanding to the simple.
Paul distinguishes the letter from the spirit: the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.
Jesus says of his own hard saying that the flesh profits nothing, and that the words he speaks are spirit and life.
The Qur'an says some of its verses are clear and others allegorical, and that those with doubt in their hearts pursue the allegorical. Who is to say which verses are which?
Origen asks who that has understanding will suppose a first, second and third day, with evening and morning, without a sun.
Jesus's warning about religious teachers is blunt: if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch.
Milton calls the negligent clergy 'blind mouths' that scarcely know how to hold a sheep-hook or anything of the herdsman's art.
Jesus charges the scribes with shutting up the kingdom of heaven against others, neither going in themselves nor letting others enter.
Newton blames the folly of interpreters who foretold times and things by prophecy and so brought the prophecy itself into contempt.
Spinoza concluded that it was as clear as the noonday light that the Pentateuch was not written by Moses. How far may reason go in examining the scripture it is asked to agree with?
Jesus accuses the scrupulous of leaving the weightier matters undone, blind guides who strain at a gnat and swallow a camel.
The psalm says that the world is established, that it cannot be moved. Is this a statement about astronomy, and what becomes of a faith that insists it is?
Jesus tells his disciples that he has many things yet to say to them which they cannot bear now.

Burke says that his countrymen cherish their old prejudices instead of casting them away, the more the longer they have lasted. Is there wisdom in inherited belief that an advancing age discards too quickly?
The Preacher insists that the thing that has been is that which shall be. What would he make of an age that claims to know more than all before it?
Solomon's wisdom took in natural knowledge: he spoke of trees from the cedar to the hyssop, and of beasts, fowl, creeping things and fishes.
Daniel is told to seal the book until the time of the end, when knowledge shall be increased.
Darwin sees open fields for far more important researches in the distant future, and light thrown on the origin of man.
Kant calls enlightenment man's release from self-incurred tutelage, the inability to use his understanding without direction from another.
The prayer which the Qur'an teaches its Prophet is for more knowledge: My Lord, increase me in knowledge.
The Preacher found that in much wisdom is much grief, and that increasing knowledge increases sorrow. What must knowledge lead to if it is not to end there?
The Qur'an says that among God's servants it is the erudite who fear him, joining learning to reverence.
Aristotle says that it is owing to their wonder that men both now begin and at first began to philosophize.
Pascal places human dignity in thought: by space the universe swallows him up like an atom, and by thought he comprehends the world.
Jesus's question weighs the two kinds of gain: what shall it profit to gain the whole world and lose one's own soul?
Thoreau calls our inventions pretty toys which distract attention from serious things, improved means to an unimproved end.
Tennyson's line marks the gap between the two kinds of progress: knowledge comes, but wisdom lingers.
Eisenhower counted every gun made, every warship launched and every rocket fired as a theft from those who hunger and are not fed.
Mill thought it questionable whether all the mechanical inventions yet made had lightened the day's toil of any human being.
Mary Shelley's Frankenstein warns by his own example how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge. Is the danger in the knowledge, or in the one who aspires beyond his nature?
Huxley held that the ethical progress of society depends not on imitating the cosmic process but on combating it.
Pascal observed that men never do evil so completely and cheerfully as when they do it from religious conviction. What must a religion be for its presence to be better than its absence?
Arnold named faith in machinery, treated as if it had a value in and for itself, the besetting danger of his age.
Mill gives a reason for independent inquiry: he who knows only his own side of the case knows little of that.
Isaiah's vision of peace has the nations beating their swords into plowshares and learning war no more.
Socrates held daily conversation about virtue, examining himself and others, to be the greatest good. Does a teaching that claims to agree with reason thereby invite such examination of itself?
Malachi argues for oneness by asking a question: have we not all one father, and has not one God created us?
Tennyson foresaw the war-drum throbbing no longer and the battle-flags furled in the parliament of man.
William James noted that showing war's irrationality and horror has no effect on its defender, for the horrors make the fascination. If reason alone does not end war, what else is needed?
Bacon warns that the human understanding is no dry light, since what a man had rather were true he more readily believes. Can science correct religion if the inquirer is not disinterested?
Habakkuk looks to an earth filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.
UNESCO's constitution places the task where the guide does: since wars begin in the minds of men, the defences of peace must be constructed there.
Milton expects much arguing and many opinions wherever there is desire to learn, for opinion in good men is knowledge in the making.
Xenophanes held that the gods did not reveal all things from the beginning, but that by seeking men find in time what is better.
Lao Tzu has a similar suspicion of multiplied words: he who knows does not care to speak, and he who is ever ready to speak does not know.
The Qur'an invites the test of repeated observation: look again at the heavens, and see whether there is any rift.
Paul holds that the invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.
Kant's two objects of awe are the starry heavens above and the moral law within. Are these two realms to be kept apart, or two views of one reality?
Keats feared that philosophy would clip an angel's wings and put the rainbow in the dull catalogue of common things. Is there a real loss in explanation that any harmony must reckon with?
The builders of Babel set out to build a city and a tower whose top may reach to heaven, and to make themselves a name.
Proverbs has an image for such mutual sharpening: iron sharpens iron, as a man sharpens the countenance of his friend.

isaiah-let-us-reason-together.text: Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord

proverbs-soul-without-knowledge.text: Also, that the soul be without knowledge, it is not good; and he that hasteth with his feet sinneth

matthew-with-all-thy-mind.text: Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind

proverbs-by-wisdom-founded-the-earth.text: The Lord by wisdom hath founded the earth; by understanding hath he established the heavens. By his knowledge the depths are broken up, and the clouds drop down the dew

quran-worst-of-beasts-deaf-dumb.text: Lo! the worst of beasts in Allah's sight are the deaf, the dumb, who have no sense.

aquinas-grace-perfects-nature.text: Since therefore grace does not destroy nature but perfects it, natural reason should minister to faith as the natural bent of the will ministers to charity
aquinas-grace-perfects-nature.author: Thomas Aquinas
aquinas-grace-perfects-nature.locator: Part I, question 1, article 8, reply to objection 2
aquinas-grace-perfects-nature.translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province

rights.note: Translation published 1920; translator Laurence Shapcote died 1947.
